content.text: Students continue building knowledge about Greek mythology by studying the Oracle as both a historical religious figure and a fictionalized guide in Percy’s world.
Myths help cultures explain danger, uncertainty, and human choices, and modern authors reinterpret those ideas for a new generation of readers.
In Lesson 17, Percy will begin making high-stakes choices on the quest, so students need today’s understanding of prophecy, fate, and structural turning points as a guide.
Students will need to compare a fictional scene with an informational source and explain how each text presents a mythic figure differently.

Part A: The Historical Oracle and the Fictional Oracle
Partner Reading & Discussion
Directions:

Read to identify key details in each text that describe the Oracle. First, reread the Oracle room scene in Chapter 9, paying close attention to the moment when Percy enters the attic and hears the prophecy. Then read
The Oracle of Delphi

, focusing on the opening paragraph that explains who the Oracle was and the sections that explain how and why people consulted her. As you read, use a Venn Diagram graphic organizer to collect one central idea from the article, one from the story, and one idea that they both share.
What is the central idea of
The Oracle of Delphi
What is one important difference between the article’s Oracle and Riordan’s Oracle?
Pulse Check
Which statement best compares the article and the novel?
A. Both texts mainly try to frighten readers with strange details about the Oracle.
B. The article explains the Oracle’s historical role in ancient Greece, while the novel turns the Oracle into a dramatic force that pushes Percy onto his quest.
C. The article and the novel both argue that prophecies should always be trusted.
D. The novel gives facts about Delphi, while the article focuses only on Percy’s feelings.
Part B: Comparing the Prophecy’s Message

Directions:

Go back to the moment the Oracle speaks, Percy’s immediate reaction, and the scene where the prophecy becomes Percy’s quest. First, think silently, then talk with your partner. After that, write a short response that explains what the prophecy says directly and what it suggests about Percy’s future.
In your written response, use one of these words
: suggests, implies,
or

. Also include one sentence that explains how Percy’s reaction helps turn the prophecy into the start of the quest.

Directions:

The Oracle of Delphi
Which phrase helped you most today when you had to move from evidence to explanation?
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the question.
Ask:
Why might a prophecy matter before anything has even happened?
An early prophecy matters because it changes how readers and characters see every next event. Even before Percy starts the quest, the warning makes his future feel more serious and more dangerous.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, we will read the Oracle scene as both a story moment and a mythic idea, then compare Riordan’s version with a factual source about the historical Oracle at Delphi.
Activate thinking about prophecy and fate, and connect Lesson 15’s work on mythic trials to Percy’s official move into quest mode.
Today’s word study supports students’ understanding of the prophecy’s warning language.
Introduce New Words Using Morphemes
Target words:
betrayed
Display and read aloud the prophecy line from Chapter 9.
“You shall be betrayed by one who calls you a friend.” (p. 141)
Say:
When a text gives us a powerful word like
betrayed
or an academic word like
historical

, we do not have to guess at its meaning. We can break the word into meaningful parts, use what we learn to build a definition, and then check that definition against the text to see if it fits. This strategy will help us to read both Percy’s story and the informational article more accurately.
Teach: Using Word parts to determine meaning
Say:
I see the word
betrayed
and notice the base
betray
and the ending
-ed
Betray
is an action word which tells me that a person’s action is a part of the prophecy.
Guide students to record:
betrayed = betray + -ed
Build a definition:

Prompt students to work with a partner to determine the meaning of the word betrayed within the context of the story. Encourage students to use word parts as well as context to infer the word’s meaning.
Verify Meaning:
Prompt students to use a dictionary or other reference material to confirm the meaning they constructed.

Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Now that we have practiced unlocking meaning with word parts, we are ready to read the article and compare its factual description of the Oracle with Riordan’s fictional version.
Teacher Tip

Before students read the Oracle scene closely, preview that Chapter 9 includes eerie fantasy imagery and a prophecy about Percy’s future. Also remind students that the Oracle comes from ancient Greek religious tradition, which we are studying as literature and history; students do not need to share the beliefs in the text in order to analyze it thoughtfully.
Check for Understanding
List the word
betrayed
in your
Personal Dictionary
. Underline the base or root word and circle each prefix and suffix. After the word, write (1) the definition of the word and (2) the definition of each focus morpheme.
Support students in using word parts and context together so they can move from a likely meaning to a precise academic meaning.
Language Focus:
Affixes and base words
Meaning statements using related to, connected to, and suggests
Before Activity
Have students say each target word aloud with a partner and then name the base word they hear inside it.
If students name only a dictionary meaning, prompt them to reconnect the meaning to the text: “How does this word function in the prophecy or article?”
Emphasize that morphology gives a smart starting point, but readers still verify meaning in context.
You said “Historical means old”—we can explain that by saying, “Historical means connected to real events or people from the past.”
You said “Betrayed means somebody is mean”—we can explain that by saying, “Betrayed means being harmed by someone who was expected to be loyal.”
The base word in ___ is ___, so I think the word means ___.
The ending ___ changes the word by showing ___.
In this text, ___ suggests ___ because ___.
Invite students to notice whether a related word exists in another language they know and to use that connection to strengthen recall of the base meaning.
Affirm student-generated word-solving strategies before refining them into more precise academic language.
If students identify a word part but cannot connect it to the sentence → Prompt: “Put your meaning back into the sentence. Does it still make sense there?”
If students confuse a base word with the whole word → Prompt: “Say the shorter word first, then add the ending. What new job does the ending do?”
Student identifies a base word or affix and uses it to make a reasonable meaning prediction.
Student revises a rough meaning into a more precise meaning after checking the sentence or reference tool.
Explicitly teach how morphemes and word parts help readers unlock meaning in key words connected to prophecy and history.
Part A: The Historical and Fictional Oracles (RI.6.2, RI.6.9) (14 minutes)

In this part of the lesson, students move between the article and Chapter 9 to compare how each text presents the Oracle. The goal is for them to identify a central idea in each source and to notice key details that support that idea. The partner routine helps them gather focused notes before shifting into deeper comparison work.
Partner Reading & Discussion
Pair students strategically. Direct partners to move between the article and Chapter 9 while locating key moments or ideas in each text.
Say these Directions:

Read to identify key details in each text that describe the Oracle. First, reread the Oracle room scene in Chapter 9, paying close attention to the moment when Percy enters the attic and hears the prophecy. Then read
The Oracle of Delphi
, focusing on the opening paragraph that explains who the Oracle was and the sections that explain how and why people consulted her. As you read, use a
Venn Diagram
graphic organizer to collect one central idea from the article, one from the story, and one idea that they both share.
Teach: Comparing a fictional story to an informational text
Say:

When I compare a story scene with an informational article, I follow a few steps. First, I ask, “What is the article mostly teaching me?” Then I ask, “What ideas are emphasized in the novel?” If both texts mention the Oracle but for different purposes, that difference helps me explain how Riordan modernizes myth rather than simply copying history. This is the kind of comparison you’ll need for the performance task.
Ask:
What is a central idea of
The Oracle of Delphi
A central idea is that the Oracle of Delphi was an important figure in ancient Greece who people believed could deliver prophecies and guide major decisions.
Ask:
What central idea or theme is conveyed through the Oracle in Chapter 9?
The Oracle scene develops the theme that prophecy creates pressure and doubt, forcing Percy to confront who he is and what kind of hero he will become—even before the quest truly begins.
Ask:
What is one important difference between the ideas in the article and Chapter 9?

The article presents the Oracle as a historical religious figure in ancient Greek culture, while Riordan presents the Oracle as a mysterious and active character in Percy’s quest. Both texts connect the Oracle to prophecy, but the novel emphasizes suspense and storytelling, while the article focuses on explanation.
Pulse Check
Which statement best compares the article and the novel?
A. Both texts mainly try to frighten readers with strange details about the Oracle.
Incorrect: A student may choose this if they focus only on the mood of Percy’s scene and ignore the article’s informational purpose.
B. The article explains the Oracle’s historical role in ancient Greece, while the novel turns the Oracle into a dramatic force that pushes Percy onto his quest.
Correct: This answer captures both the article’s central idea and the novel’s different purpose in presenting the same figure.
C. The article and the novel both argue that prophecies should always be trusted.
Incorrect: A student may choose this if they confuse description with argument and overstate what either text claims.
D. The novel gives facts about Delphi, while the article focuses only on Percy’s feelings.
Incorrect: This reverses the roles of the texts and shows confusion about genre.
Support students in explaining how two texts present the same figure differently by using comparison and central-idea language.
Language Focus:
Comparison transitions
Central-idea frames
Academic nouns such as significance, priestess, and prophecy
Before Activity
Have students orally rehearse one sentence beginning with “The article emphasizes . . .” and one sentence beginning with “In contrast, the novel emphasizes . . .”
If students start listing details without synthesis, redirect with: “What do those details add up to in the article?”
Prompt students to use domain vocabulary from the article instead of vague labels like thing or person.
You said “The article tells facts”—we can explain that by saying, “The article emphasizes the Oracle’s historical significance in ancient Greek culture.”
You said “The book makes it creepy”—we can explain that by saying, “The novel presents the Oracle as an eerie guide whose prophecy drives the plot forward.”
The central idea of the article is that ___.
Both texts present the Oracle as ___, but the article emphasizes ___ whereas the novel emphasizes ___.
This difference matters because ___.
Allow students to discuss the comparison first in a shared home language, if helpful, and then restate the idea in English using one comparison stem.
Encourage students to bring in prior knowledge from Lessons 1–3 about how myths can explain the unknown and how modern authors transform older stories for a new generation of readers.
If students confuse a central idea with one detail → Prompt: “Can your sentence cover the whole article, not just one section?”
If students compare only surface details → Prompt: “What larger purpose does each author have for including the Oracle?”
Student states a central idea broad enough to cover the full informational text.
Student uses a comparison word to explain a meaningful difference in presentation, not just a small visual detail.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Determining Central Idea

Have students complete this frame before sharing: “The article is mostly about ___ because it explains ___ and ___.” Making a Meaningful Comparison: Ask students to name each text’s purpose first and then compare the purposes rather than isolated details.
Ready for extension

Add a second difference explaining how the article centers on ancient Greek culture while Riordan centers on Percy’s point of view. Invite students to explain how this comparison connects back to Lesson 3’s idea of myth adaptation.
Part B: Comparing the Prophecy’s Message (RL.6.9) (16 minutes)
Think-Pair-Write-Share

In this part of the lesson, students revisit three key moments—the prophecy itself, Percy’s reaction, and the moment the quest becomes official—to help them see how fate and choice start to intersect. The Think‑Pair‑Write‑Share routine gives them time to process the literal message of the prophecy and its deeper implications before writing a short explanation.
Keep students anchored in three key moments: when Percy hears the prophecy, when he reacts to it, and when the quest becomes official.
Say these Directions:

Go back to the moment the Oracle speaks, Percy’s immediate reaction, and the scene where the prophecy becomes Percy’s quest. First, think silently, then talk with your partner. After that, write a short response that explains what the prophecy says directly and what it suggests about Percy’s future.
In your written response, use one of these words
: suggests, implies,
or
symbolizes
. Also include one sentence that explains how Percy’s reaction helps turn the prophecy into the start of the quest.

The prophecy says Percy will go on a quest to return something that was stolen and that someone he trusts will betray him. It also says he won’t be able to save what matters most. This suggests his journey will be dangerous and kind of sad, and it implies he will have to make hard choices. Percy is confused and a little scared when he hears it, but he still agrees to go on the quest, which helps turn the prophecy into the start of his journey.
Teach: Analyzing Symbolism
Say:
A prophecy works on two levels. One level is
literal
—the words name events or people Percy may meet. The other level is
symbolic

—the words hint at danger, betrayal, and choices before Percy fully understands them. When Percy reacts with confusion but still has to move forward, the prophecy becomes a pivotal moment: it ends his camp-only life and opens the official hero’s quest. That is how fate begins to feel unavoidable in the story.
Support students in moving from evidence to interpretation by explaining how symbolic language in the prophecy suggests larger ideas about fate and Percy’s future.
Language Focus:
Symbolism sentence structures
Implication language
Cause-and-effect reasoning
Before Activity
Display and practice these two frames orally: “The image of ___ suggests ___ because ___” and “Percy’s reaction matters because ___.”
If students cite a prophecy line but stop there, ask: “What future possibility does that detail point to?”
Reinforce that interpretation must stay connected to the text; students should not guess wildly beyond what the prophecy suggests.
You said “It means something bad”—we can explain that by saying, “The prophecy implies that Percy’s quest will include danger he cannot fully control.”
You said “The friend part is a clue”—we can explain that by saying, “The warning about a friend symbolizes future conflict built around trust and betrayal.”
The prophecy directly states ___, but it also implies ___.
The symbol of ___ suggests ___ because ___.
Percy’s reaction helps launch the quest because ___.
Invite students to connect the idea of symbolic warning language to stories, sayings, or oral traditions they already know, if they choose, while keeping the explanation grounded in today’s text.
Affirm interpretive thinking by valuing multiple text-based meanings before guiding students toward the strongest supported explanation.
If students list separate details without explaining the connection to fate → Prompt: “What do these clues add up to about Percy’s future?”
If students confuse symbolic meaning with unsupported prediction → Prompt: “Which exact word in the prophecy gives you that idea?”
Student uses a verb such as suggests, implies, or symbolizes to connect a prophecy detail to a larger idea.
Student explains Percy’s reaction as part of the plot shift rather than only summarizing what the prophecy says.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Moving from Evidence to Interpretation

Offer this frame: “The prophecy says ___, which suggests ___ because ___.” Writing the Response: Allow students to say their sentence aloud to a partner first, record it orally, or use speech-to-text before writing.
Ready for extension

Ask students to explain how the prophecy connects to the Greek cultural idea of Fate and whether Riordan presents that idea as fixed or partly shaped by Percy’s choices. Invite students to compare the Oracle’s warning to another mythic warning from earlier lessons and explain a shared pattern.
Part A: The Historical and Fictional Oracles (RI.6.2, RI.6.9)
Students will determine the central idea of the article and compare the article’s presentation of the Oracle to Riordan’s version in Chapter 9.
Part B: Comparing the Prophecy’s Message (RL.6.5)
Students will analyze Percy’s reaction to the prophecy and explain how symbolic language and implied meaning make fate seem unavoidable and launch the quest.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
Respond in writing to the following prompt:
How do the novel and the article present the Oracle differently? Use at least two specific details—one from Percy’s prophecy scene and one from The Oracle of Delphi.
Ask:

SAMPLE RESPONSE: The article presents the Oracle as a historical priestess whose messages mattered in ancient Greek life. In contrast, Riordan turns the Oracle into a spooky story figure whose prophecy launches Percy’s quest. The warning about betrayal makes fate feel unavoidable because Percy hears about future danger before he can choose his path, so the quest feels planned for him even as he has to live it.
Performance Task Bridge
Say:

Today you practiced a skill you will need for the performance task: comparing a fictional scene with an informational source. When you explain how Riordan adapts a traditional myth idea, you are practicing the same kind of thinking you will use in the final unit task. Keep noticing not just what stays the same across texts, but why an author changes it for modern readers.
Ask:
Which phrase helped you most today when you had to move from evidence to explanation?
The phrase that helped me most was “suggests that” because it pushed me to explain the meaning of the prophecy instead of just repeating it.
Students will synthesize ideas across both texts in a brief evidence-based
Quick Write
connected to the performance task.
Have students access their copy of
The Lightning Thief
. Instruct students to:
Read the summary of Chapter 10, pp. 149–157.
Read and annotate
The Lightning Thief
, Chapter 10, pp. 158–167, looking for Percy’s first major decisions as the quest begins.
